directions: Start seed indoors 12-14 weeks before the last frost, as this pubescens type is notoriously slow to germinate and needs a long season to mature its blocky, irregularly shaped fruit. Pods hold black seeds and thick, juicy flesh typical of rocoto, ripening to a bright yellow with heat ranging from moderate to fiercely hot (roughly 10,000-60,000 Scoville units). Plants form a more compact bush than typical rocoto and, like other pubescens types, set fruit best where summer nights stay relatively cool.

planting.note: Sow indoors 12-14 weeks ahead of the last frost; performs best with some afternoon relief from peak summer heat, since pubescens sets fruit poorly above roughly 90°F.

directions: Sow indoors 12-14 weeks ahead of the last frost, giving this rare rocoto selection the long, patient start every pubescens variety demands. Medium-sized fruits mature to a distinctive chocolate-brown, with the thick, crunchy walls and fruity, apple-like heat characteristic of the species. Because pubescens sets fruit poorly above roughly 90°F, plants perform best with some afternoon relief from peak summer heat in hot-summer regions.

planting.note: Start indoors 12-14 weeks before the last frost, well ahead of standard peppers, since pubescens seed is slow and erratic to germinate.

directions: Start indoors 12-14 weeks before the last frost, well ahead of standard peppers, since pubescens seed is slow and erratic to germinate. Unlike the round, apple-shaped manzano rocoto, the Perón type produces elongated, pear-shaped pods with thick, juicy walls that hold up especially well to stuffing and roasting. Deep purple flowers and fuzzy, hairy foliage distinguish the plant from every other cultivated pepper species, and it tolerates cooler nights better than typical warm-season chiles.

planting.note: Start seed indoors 8-10 weeks before the last frost and transplant once soil has warmed.

directions: Start seed indoors 8-10 weeks before the last frost and transplant once soil has warmed. Bred at Auburn University in the 1970s to replace tobacco-mosaic-susceptible stock, this cultivar produces the same slender, upward-facing, fiery fruit as classic tabasco but on virus-resistant plants, making it a more dependable choice for home growers and small producers. Pods ripen from pale yellow through orange to red, and are traditionally mashed and aged into vinegar-based hot sauce, though they work equally well fresh or dried.

common_name: Siling Labuyo Pepper (Philippine Bird's Eye Chili)

planting.note: Start seed indoors 8-10 weeks before the last frost; harvest frequently to keep the compact, heavily branching bush setting new fruit.

directions: Start seed indoors 8-10 weeks before the last frost; this Filipino landrace grows into a shrubby perennial in frost-free climates but performs well as a warm-season annual elsewhere. The tiny, tapering pods — among the smallest of any cultivated chile — pack intense heat around 80,000-100,000 Scoville units and are used both fresh and dried in staples like sinigang, bicol express, and vinegar-based dipping sauces; young leaves are also edible and used in some regional dishes. Harvest frequently to keep the compact, heavily branching bush setting new fruit.
sources: Slow Food Foundation — Ark of Taste

common_name: Kanthari Chili Pepper (Kerala Bird's Eye Chili)

planting.note: Start seed indoors 8-10 weeks before the last frost; productive and heat-tolerant, setting clusters of two to three fruits per node.

directions: Start seed indoors 8-10 weeks before the last frost; this compact, bushy frutescens landrace from Kerala, India, is prized in South Indian cooking for its small, marble-round, glossy red pods. Heat runs high (roughly 50,000-100,000 Scoville units) but dissipates faster than many other hot peppers, leaving a bright, citrusy flavor that's central to Kerala fish curries, chutneys, and pickles. Plants are productive and heat-tolerant, setting clusters of two to three fruits per node through a long harvest season.
